name: Major World Religions & Philosophies
summary: Historical branches and genealogy of the world's primary faith traditions and philosophical frameworks, organized by origin and historical progression.
coreBeliefs: Diverse understandings of the divine, spiritual realm, and human purpose.
Guidelines for ethical conduct and community cohesion.
Frameworks for addressing existential questions of life, death, and suffering.
historicalBackground: Religious beliefs and practices have existed since the dawn of human consciousness. Animism, shamanism, and ancestral worship represent early forms of human spirituality, leading to organized systems following the agricultural revolution.

children.name: Indigenous & Folk Religions
children.summary: Traditional belief systems of indigenous peoples globally, strongly tied to ancestral lands, animism, and tribal lineages.
coreBeliefs: Animism: Spiritual forces reside in all natural entities (plants, rocks, rivers).
Ancestor veneration: Deceased ancestors act as guardians and intermediaries.
Sacred geography: Deep spiritual connections to specific ancestral lands.
Shamanism: Spiritual leaders communicate with the spirit world for healing and guidance.
children.historicalBackground: These represent the oldest spiritual traditions of humanity, pre-dating written history. They have survived centuries of colonialism and missionary efforts, often syncretizing with global religions.

children.name: African Traditional Religions
children.summary: The diverse indigenous religions of sub-Saharan Africa, centered on a supreme creator deity, ancestor worship, and elemental spirits.
scriptures: Oral narratives (e.g., Odu Ifa in Yoruba)
coreBeliefs: Belief in a high creator God alongside lesser deities (Orishas/spirits).
Ancestral veneration: Spirits of ancestors remain active in the community.
Vital force: Cosmic energy flowing through all living things.
children.historicalBackground: Developed organically over millennia in Africa, these systems heavily influenced African diaspora religions (such as Santeria, Candomble, and Haitian Vodou) through the transatlantic slave trade.

children.name: Yoruba Religion
children.summary: The indigenous spiritual system of the Yoruba people of Nigeria and Benin, centered on the creator Olodumare and intermediary spirits called Orishas.
coreBeliefs: Olodumare is the supreme creator deity.
Orishas represent aspects of nature and human behavior.
Destiny (Ayanmo) can be navigated through Ifa divination.
children.historicalBackground: Centered in Ile-Ife, Yoruba religion formed a complex priestly hierarchy that was later carried to the Americas, serving as the theological backbone for Santeria in Cuba and Candomblé in Brazil.

children.name: Vodun (West African)
children.summary: The indigenous religion of the Fon and Ewe peoples of Benin and Togo, focusing on divine spirits (Mawu-Lisa) and ancestor guardians.
coreBeliefs: Mawu-Lisa is the supreme dual deity (sun and moon).
Spirits (Vodun) govern natural elements and human destiny.
Direct communication with spirits through trance state.
children.historicalBackground: Originating in coastal West Africa, Vodun was formalized in the Kingdom of Dahomey. It is recognized as an official religion in Benin, where it retains massive cultural and legal significance.

children.name: Akan Religion
children.summary: The indigenous monotheistic and animistic beliefs of the Akan people of Ghana and Ivory Coast, featuring a supreme god Nyame and earth spirits.
coreBeliefs: Nyame is the omnipotent creator God.
Abosom are lesser deities/nature spirits acting as Nyame's helpers.
Asase Yaa is the earth goddess of agriculture and fertility.
children.historicalBackground: Central to the social structures of the Ashanti Empire, Akan beliefs shaped their resistance to British colonization and are preserved in cultural festivals and Adinkra symbolism.

children.name: Dinka Religion
children.summary: The traditional pastoralist religion of the Dinka people of South Sudan, centered on the supreme creator deity Nhialic.
coreBeliefs: Nhialic is the creator God associated with sky and rain.
Spirits (Jok) can cause illness or bring fortune.
Sacred relationship with cattle, which are indicators of spiritual status.
children.historicalBackground: Maintained by the Dinka pastoralists for centuries along the Nile, surviving Islamic expansion and Christianization efforts.

children.name: San Religion
children.summary: The ancient hunter-gatherer belief system of the San (Bushmen) peoples of Southern Africa, featuring a creator god and trance dancing.
coreBeliefs: Belief in a creator God and a trickster deity.
Trance dance: Accessing spiritual energy (n/um) for healing.
Interconnectedness between humans, animals, and stars.
children.historicalBackground: Representing some of the oldest continuous human cultures, San rock art dating back tens of thousands of years depicts spiritual trance dances that are still practiced today.

children.name: Native American Religions
children.summary: The diverse spiritual systems of the indigenous peoples of the Americas, characterized by connection to the earth, animal spirits, and ancestral guidance.
coreBeliefs: Great Spirit / Great Mystery: A divine unifying force in the universe.
Living in harmony with all creations (animals, plants, winds).
Sacredness of local geographies and natural landmarks.
Reciprocal relationship with the spirit world.
children.historicalBackground: Developed in isolation across the Americas. Following European contact, these religions faced severe suppression, leading to syncretic movements and revitalization efforts in the 20th century.

children.name: Navajo Religion
children.summary: The traditional belief system of the Diné (Navajo) of the American Southwest, focused on maintaining Hózhó (harmony, beauty, and balance).
coreBeliefs: Hózhó: The cosmic state of balance and beauty.
Holy People (Diyin Diné): Supernatural beings who created the Navajo world.
Disease is caused by disharmony or violating taboos.
children.historicalBackground: Diverged from Athabaskan roots, incorporating Pueblo agricultural ceremonies. It survived the Navajo Long Walk of 1864 and continues to shape Navajo tribal life.

children.name: Lakota Religion
children.summary: The traditional spirituality of the Lakota (Sioux) people of the Great Plains, centered on Wakan Tanka (the Great Mystery).
coreBeliefs: Wakan Tanka: The supreme, unfathomable sacred unity.
Mitakuye Oyasin: 'All my relations' - everything in the cosmos is interconnected.
White Buffalo Calf Woman brought the sacred pipe to teach humans how to pray.
children.historicalBackground: A nomadic Great Plains religion that integrated buffalo hunting into its spiritual cycle. Banned by the US government in the late 19th century, the practices were kept alive secretly until the American Indian Religious Freedom Act of 1978.

children.name: Maya Religion
children.summary: The polytheistic, state-sponsored religion of the historical Maya civilization, centered on astronomical cycles, agricultural gods, and blood sacrifice.
children.followersEstimate: Extinct as state religion; millions practice folk syncretic forms
coreBeliefs: The universe is divided into earth, heaven (13 layers), and underworld (Xibalba, 9 layers).
Deities control rain, maize, war, and time (e.g., Kukulkan, Chaac).
Time operates in cyclical cosmic rounds.
children.historicalBackground: Built complex pyramid temples and calendars. Survived the classic collapse of cities, but faced systematic destruction of codices by Spanish Bishop Diego de Landa in 1562.

children.name: Aztec Religion
children.summary: The state religion of the Aztec Empire, focused on maintaining cosmic balance through warfare and human sacrifice to feed the sun god Huitzilopochtli.
children.followersEstimate: Extinct as state religion; cultural revitalization groups exist
coreBeliefs: Dualism: Ometeotl represents the supreme creative dual force (male/female).
Sun requires human hearts (chalchihuatl) to battle the dark forces of night.
We live in the fifth cosmic era (the Fifth Sun).
children.historicalBackground: Consolidated under Moctezuma and Tlacaelel. Tenochtitlan temple complexes fell to Hernan Cortes in 1521, causing immediate state dissolution.

children.name: Inca Religion
children.summary: The state religion of the Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu), centered on the sun god Inti and the creator Viracocha.
children.followersEstimate: Extinct as state religion; millions practice syncretic Andean folk religion
coreBeliefs: Inti is the sun ancestor of the royal Inca dynasty.
Viracocha is the transcendent creator god.
Huacas (sacred locations/stones/mountains) possess spiritual energy.
children.historicalBackground: Centralized under Pachacuti. Coricancha (Temple of the Sun) in Cuzco was the spiritual heart. Destroyed by Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro in 1533.

children.name: Australian Aboriginal Religions
children.summary: The animistic and totemistic beliefs of the indigenous peoples of Australia, centered on the Dreamtime (Creation Era).
coreBeliefs: The Dreamtime: The continuous, sacred era of creation when ancestral spirits shaped the landscape.
Songlines: Navigational pathways mapped across Australia using sacred stories.
Totemism: Spiritual bonds between individuals and specific animal/plant species.
children.historicalBackground: Representing the oldest continuous religious tradition on Earth, dating back over 50,000 years. Songlines allowed survival across the desert by embedding water coordinates in sacred songs.

children.name: Polynesian Religions
children.summary: The traditional animistic religions of the Pacific Islands, centered on Mana (spiritual power) and Tapu (sacred restrictions).
coreBeliefs: Mana: Supernatural spiritual power residing in people, places, and objects.
Tapu (Taboo): Spiritual laws of prohibition to protect Mana.
Atua: Deities who control nature (e.g. Kane, Lono, Tangaroa).
children.historicalBackground: Developed during the navigation and settlement of Pacific islands. Strongly tied to chieftain lineage and naval navigation cosmology.

children.name: Māori Religion
children.summary: The traditional spiritual beliefs of the Māori of New Zealand, centered on ancestors and forest gods like Tāne.
coreBeliefs: Ranginui (Sky Father) and Papatūānuku (Earth Mother) are the primordial parents.
Mauri: Life force present in all creations.
Whakapapa: Genealogy linking all humans to the gods.
children.historicalBackground: Developed after East Polynesian travelers settled New Zealand. It shaped tribal warfare, tattooing (Tā moko), and is preserved in modern Māori activism and cultural rights.

children.name: Hawaiian Religion
children.summary: The traditional religion of Native Hawaiians, featuring volcanic gods like Pele and strict Kapu laws.
coreBeliefs: Pele is the volcanic goddess of fire and creation.
The Kapu system regulates spiritual hygiene and caste structures.
Four primary gods: Kū, Lono, Kāne, Kanaloa.
children.historicalBackground: A highly structured temple state. King Kamehameha II abolished the Kapu system in 1819, and American missionaries quickly converted most of the population, leaving traditional elements preserved in hula and mythology.

children.name: Samoan Traditions
children.summary: The traditional spiritual beliefs of the Samoan people, centered on the creator Tagaloa and family spirits (Aitu).
coreBeliefs: Tagaloa is the supreme god of the heavens.
Aitu represent ancestor spirits that can intervene in the material world.
Sacred social hierarchy based on the matai (chief) system.
children.historicalBackground: Deeply syncretized with Christianity in the 19th century, forming 'Fa'a Samoa' (the Samoan way), where traditional protocols and family authority remain supreme.

children.name: Siberian Religions
children.summary: The classical shamanic religions of the indigenous peoples of Northern Asia, featuring cosmic trees and soul flight.
coreBeliefs: Shaman: The exclusive specialist who journeys to upper/lower worlds in trance.
World Tree (Axis Mundi) connects the heavens, earth, and underworld.
Spirit helpers assist the shaman in healing and weather control.
children.historicalBackground: This region is the linguistic source of the term 'shaman'. Despite Soviet anti-religious campaigns, shamanism saw a massive resurgence in post-Soviet Russia.

children.name: Arctic Religions
children.summary: The traditional animistic beliefs of the Inuit and other Arctic peoples, centered on ocean spirits and animal soul respect.
coreBeliefs: Sedna is the goddess of the sea who controls marine mammals.
Anirniit: Everything has a soul, requiring ritual respect when hunting.
Sila: The breath of life and the cosmic weather spirit.
children.historicalBackground: Shaped by the harsh polar environment, these practices established hunting taboos to preserve animal populations and appease sea and land spirits.

children.name: Abrahamic Religions
children.summary: Monotheistic faiths tracing their spiritual lineage back to the Hebrew patriarch Abraham, characterized by linear time, scriptures, and covenants.
coreBeliefs: Monotheism: Belief in one supreme, creator God.
Covenantal Relationship: A historic alliance between God and humanity.
Prophethood: God communicates through divine messengers.
Linear Time: History moves from creation toward final judgment and redemption.
children.historicalBackground: Emerging from ancient Semitic populations in the Middle East, these religions evolved through a series of covenants, revelations, and reforms, shaping Western and Middle Eastern history.

children.name: Judaism
children.summary: The ancient monotheistic religion, culture, and legal tradition of the Jewish people, rooted in the covenant between God and the Children of Israel.
coreBeliefs: One indivisible God who is the creator of the universe.
The covenant established at Mount Sinai between God and the Israelites.
Observation of the Mitzvot (613 commandments) to live righteously.
Tikkun Olam: The ethical duty to repair the world.
children.historicalBackground: Judaism began as the national faith of the Israelites. Following the destruction of the Second Temple in Jerusalem (70 CE), it transitioned into Rabbinic Judaism, centering on study, prayer, and synagogues.

children.name: Orthodox Judaism
children.summary: A branch of Rabbinic Judaism that advocates for the strict adherence to Halakha (Jewish Law) as historically inherited, viewing it as divine and unchanging.
coreBeliefs: Torah min HaShamayim: The Torah is literally divine in origin.
The absolute and binding authority of Halakha.
Traditional preservation of liturgy and gender roles.
children.historicalBackground: Coalesced in response to the Haskalah (Jewish Enlightenment) and Reform movements, asserting the enduring authority of traditional law.

children.name: Reform Judaism
children.summary: A major denominational branch characterized by a progressive approach to Jewish law, emphasis on ethical commandments over ritual laws, and adaptation to modern culture.
coreBeliefs: The Torah is a historically evolving record of revelation.
Individual autonomy in deciding which ritual practices to observe.
Strong focus on social justice and interfaith dialogue (Tikkun Olam).
Full gender equality and inclusion in all ritual practices.
children.historicalBackground: Began in Germany to align Jewish practice with modern European citizenship, later expanding and developing its primary base in North America.
holidays: Biblical festivals with emphasis on ethical messages

children.name: Conservative Judaism
children.summary: A moderate stream of Judaism that seeks to conserve Jewish tradition while allowing for modification in light of contemporary realities.
scriptures: Responsa of the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards
coreBeliefs: Halakha is evolving and historically conditioned, but still binding.
Integration of critical academic research with Jewish practice.
Equality of men and women in ritual services.
children.historicalBackground: Formed as a middle ground between Reform and Orthodox positions in 19th-century Germany, finding its largest representation in 20th-century America.

children.name: Reconstructionist Judaism
children.summary: A modern American Jewish movement that views Judaism as an evolving religious civilization rather than a set of theological dogmas.
coreBeliefs: Judaism is a cultural and religious civilization.
Rejection of the traditional concept of the 'chosen people'.
Halakha is not binding law but valuable folkways and traditions.
children.historicalBackground: Developed out of Conservative Judaism under Mordecai Kaplan, emphasizing community centers and the integration of democratic values into Jewish practice.

children.name: Karaite Judaism
children.summary: An ancient branch of Judaism that rejects the Oral Law (Talmud) and asserts that the Tanakh is the sole source of divine law.
coreBeliefs: Absolute authority of the Written Torah.
Rejection of rabbinic authority and talmudic additions.
Individual responsibility to interpret the biblical text directly.
children.historicalBackground: Coalesced in the Abbasid Caliphate as a theological challenge to the Rabbinic academies of Sura and Pumbedita. It spread to Egypt, the Byzantine Empire, and Crimea.

children.name: Humanistic Judaism
children.summary: A modern non-theistic movement that defines Judaism as the cultural and historical experience of the Jewish people, rather than divine covenant.
coreBeliefs: Non-theism: Human reason and action solve problems, not divine intervention.
Jewish identity is defined by culture, heritage, and history.
Ethical behavior must be rooted in human needs and rights.
children.historicalBackground: Founded in Detroit by Rabbi Sherwin Wine to accommodate secular Jews who desired a Jewish connection without theistic creeds.
holidays: Hanukkah with focus on human courage

children.name: Christianity
children.summary: A major monotheistic religion based on the life, teachings, death, and resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth, whom followers believe to be the Messiah (Christ) and the Son of God.
coreBeliefs: The Trinity: God exists as three co-equal, co-eternal persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit).
Salvation: Through faith in Jesus' sacrificial death and resurrection.
Incarnation: Jesus is fully divine and fully human.
The Second Coming: Christ will return to judge the living and the dead.
children.historicalBackground: Began as a Jewish sect within Roman Palestine. It spread throughout the Roman Empire, eventually becoming the state religion in the 4th century. Subsequent schisms divided the Church into Eastern and Western branches.

children.name: Catholicism
children.summary: The largest Christian church, headed by the Bishop of Rome (the Pope), asserting apostolic succession from Saint Peter.
coreBeliefs: Papal Infallibility: The Pope is preserved from error when teaching ex cathedra on faith and morals.
Seven Sacraments: Channels of divine grace.
Transubstantiation: The bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ.
Purgatory: A state of purification before entering heaven.
children.historicalBackground: The history of Catholicism is central to Western civilization. Key turning points include the Councils of Nicaea, the Great Schism of 1054, the Protestant Reformation, and the Second Vatican Council (Vatican II).

children.name: Latin Church (Roman Rite)
children.summary: The largest autonomous particular church of the Catholic Church, practicing Western liturgies and led directly by the Pope.
coreBeliefs: Clerical celibacy as standard discipline.
Use of the Latin theological and liturgical tradition.
Universal jurisdiction of the Bishop of Rome.
children.historicalBackground: Formed the cultural framework of medieval Western Europe, spreading globally via Spanish, Portuguese, and French exploration and colonial expansion.

children.name: Eastern Catholic Churches
children.summary: Twenty-three eastern rite self-governing churches in full communion with the Pope, preserving Eastern theological and liturgical traditions.
coreBeliefs: Full papal supremacy and Catholic dogmas.
Permissibility of married priests (standard eastern discipline).
Preservation of Eastern liturgies and liturgical languages.
children.historicalBackground: Formed when sections of Eastern Orthodox or Oriental Orthodox churches sought reunion with Rome, agreeing to papal authority while keeping their historical liturgies.
practices: Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom

children.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
children.summary: The second-largest Christian church, comprised of self-governing national bodies that preserve the liturgical and theological traditions of the Eastern Roman Empire (Byzantium).
coreBeliefs: Theosis: The ultimate goal of Christian life is deification/union with God.
Conciliarity: The church is governed by bishops in ecumenical councils, with no single supreme leadership.
Sacred Tradition: Perfect preservation of early Christian doctrine and liturgy.
Veneration of Icons: Holy images serve as windows into the spiritual realm.
children.historicalBackground: Centered in Constantinople, the Eastern Church diverged from Rome over theological questions like the filioque clause and papal supremacy, culminating in the Great Schism.

children.name: Greek Orthodox
children.summary: The self-governing bodies of Eastern Orthodoxy that conduct their services in Greek and inherit the Byzantine heritage.
coreBeliefs: The Ecumenical Patriarch is first among equals (primus inter pares).
Adherence to the seven ecumenical councils.
Preservation of Koine Greek in theological study and liturgy.
children.historicalBackground: Inherited the direct cultural legacy of the Eastern Roman Empire. The fall of Constantinople in 1553 shifted its political context but preserved its liturgical hierarchy.

children.name: Russian Orthodox
children.summary: The largest autocephalous Eastern Orthodox church, established in Kievan Rus' and led by the Patriarch of Moscow.
coreBeliefs: Moscow as the 'Third Rome' (historical concept of leadership).
Monastic spirituality focused on elders (Starsty).
Deep integration of liturgy with Russian cultural identity.
children.historicalBackground: Vladimir the Great adopted Orthodoxy in 988. The church grew into a massive national institution, survived severe Bolshevik repression in the 20th century, and saw a post-Soviet revival.

children.name: Serbian Orthodox
children.summary: An autocephalous Eastern Orthodox church representing the Serbian people, centered in Belgrade.
coreBeliefs: Svetosavlje: The Serbian national synthesis of Orthodoxy led by St. Sava.
Veneration of national saints and royalty.
Liturgy in Serbian and Church Slavonic.
children.historicalBackground: Founded by Saint Sava, who secured church independence from Byzantium. It served as the key preserver of Serbian language and identity during centuries of Ottoman rule.

children.name: Oriental Orthodoxy
children.summary: A family of autocephalous Eastern churches that rejected the Council of Chalcedon (451 CE), adhering to miaphysite christology.
children.geographicOrigin: Egypt, Armenia, Syria, Horn of Africa
coreBeliefs: Miaphysitism: Jesus Christ has one unified divine-human nature (physis).
Rejection of the Council of Chalcedon's 'two natures' formula.
Apostolic succession and sacramental theology.
children.historicalBackground: Separated from Roman and Byzantine churches after 451 CE due to semantic and theological differences over Christ's nature. Developed in isolation under Islamic rule.

children.name: Coptic Orthodox
children.summary: The indigenous Christian church of Egypt, led by the Pope of Alexandria, tracing its origin to Saint Mark.
coreBeliefs: Alexandrian theological school supremacy.
Preservation of monastic leadership traditions.
Miaphysite Christological definition.
children.historicalBackground: Founded by St. Mark in Alexandria. Coptic Christians faced persecution under Roman, Byzantine, and Islamic rulers, preserving their distinct Coptic language (derived from ancient Egyptian).

children.name: Armenian Apostolic
children.summary: The national church of Armenia, which was the first nation to adopt Christianity as its state religion.
coreBeliefs: National identity tied directly to church membership.
Adherence to Cyril of Alexandria's theology.
Miaphysitism.
children.historicalBackground: King Tiridates III converted in 301 CE under St. Gregory's influence. The church created the Armenian alphabet (by Mesrop Mashtots) to translate scriptures, preserving national identity during centuries of division.

children.name: Ethiopian Orthodox
children.summary: The largest Oriental Orthodox church, located in the Horn of Africa, characterized by unique Semitic and Old Testament influences.
scriptures: Ethiopic Biblical Canon (81 books - largest in Christendom)
coreBeliefs: Tabot: Reverence for replicas of the Ark of the Covenant in every church.
Strict dietary laws matching biblical Kashrut/Halal.
Observance of Saturday Sabbath alongside Sunday Lord's Day.
children.historicalBackground: Adopted under Axumite King Ezana. Remained isolated in the highlands of Africa, preserving ancient liturgies and the Ge'ez language.

children.name: Protestantism
children.summary: A major branch of Christianity originating with the 16th-century Reformation, rejecting papal authority and emphasizing salvation by grace alone through faith.
coreBeliefs: Sola Scriptura: The Bible alone is the final authority for Christian faith and life.
Sola Fide: Salvation is received through faith alone, apart from good works.
Sola Gratia: Salvation is entirely a free gift of God's grace.
Priesthood of All Believers: All Christians have direct access to God without priestly mediation.
children.historicalBackground: Began when Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses in Wittenberg, Germany, protesting Catholic sales of indulgences. The movement spread rapidly across Northern Europe, fragmenting into diverse theological streams.

children.name: Lutheranism
children.summary: The oldest Protestant branch, based directly on the theological reforms of Martin Luther, focusing on justification by faith.
coreBeliefs: Justification by grace through faith alone.
Sacramental union in the Eucharist (consubstantiation).
The Two Kingdoms doctrine of spiritual and worldly authority.
children.historicalBackground: The root movement of the Protestant Reformation. Luther's refusal to recant his writings at the Diet of Worms led to the division of Western Christianity.

children.name: Anglicanism
children.summary: A Christian tradition representing the middle path (via media) between Catholicism and Protestantism, originating from the Church of England.
coreBeliefs: Apostolic succession retained without papal authority.
Liturgy in the vernacular combining Catholic sacrament and Protestant reform.
Three-legged stool of authority: Scripture, Tradition, and Reason.
children.historicalBackground: Established when King Henry VIII declared independence from Rome via the Act of Supremacy. Archbishop Thomas Cranmer compiled the liturgical Book of Common Prayer.
practices: Liturgical Book of Common Prayer services

children.name: Reformed (Calvinism)
children.summary: A Protestant tradition based on the theology of John Calvin, emphasizing the absolute sovereignty of God and predestination.
coreBeliefs: Absolute Sovereignty of God in all aspects of creation.
Predestination: God has elect individuals chosen for salvation before the foundation of the world.
TULIP: Total Depravity, Unconditional Election, Limited Atonement, Irresistible Grace, Perseverance of the Saints.
children.historicalBackground: Developed in Geneva, Switzerland, Calvin's systematic theology spread to France, the Netherlands, Scotland (via John Knox), and England, heavily influencing the Puritans.

children.name: Methodism
children.summary: A Protestant branch originating in 18th-century England, emphasizing social holiness, missionary work, and systematic study.
coreBeliefs: Prevenient grace: God's grace is active in all humans before conversion.
Christian perfection: The possibility of achieving complete love in this life.
Arminian theology: Salvation is available to all, rejecting predestination.
children.historicalBackground: Began as a revival movement within the Church of England led by brothers John and Charles Wesley. They structured their followers into 'societies' or 'classes' using a methodical approach.

children.name: Baptist Churches
children.summary: A Protestant group characterized by the practice of believer's baptism by immersion and the autonomy of local congregations.
coreBeliefs: Believer's Baptism: Baptism is reserved for those who can make a conscious profession of faith.
Soul Competency: Direct individual responsibility before God.
Autonomy of the local church: No hierarchy; each church is self-governing.
children.historicalBackground: Emerged out of English Separatism. John Smyth baptized himself and his congregation in Amsterdam in 1609. The movement spread to the American colonies, growing massive in the South.

children.name: Pentecostalism
children.summary: A modern Protestant movement emphasizing direct personal experience of God through baptism with the Holy Spirit and spiritual gifts.
coreBeliefs: Baptism with the Holy Spirit as an experience distinct from water baptism.
Speaking in tongues (glossolalia) as initial physical evidence.
Active continuation of spiritual gifts (healing, prophecy, miracles).
children.historicalBackground: Traced to the Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles (1906) led by African-American preacher William J. Seymour, which catalyzed a global expansion.

children.name: Seventh-day Adventism
children.summary: A Protestant branch distinguished by its observance of Saturday as the Sabbath and its emphasis on the imminent second coming (Advent) of Jesus Christ.
scriptures: Writings of Ellen G. White (prophetic status)
coreBeliefs: Observance of the seventh-day Sabbath (Saturday) as a holy day.
The heavenly sanctuary doctrine and investigative judgment.
Condition of the dead: Soul sleep (unconsciousness) until resurrection.
Holistic health: Promoting vegetarianism and abstaining from alcohol/clean lifestyle.
children.historicalBackground: Emerged from the Millerite movement in New York after the 'Great Disappointment' of 1844 when Jesus did not return. Ellen G. White's writings provided the theological consolidation.

children.name: Restorationist Churches
children.summary: A broad category of Christian movements originating during the Second Great Awakening, asserting a restoration of primitive, apostolic Christianity rather than reform.
coreBeliefs: Rejection of traditional post-biblical creedal orthodoxies.
Restoration of original church offices, structure, and spiritual authority.
Varying non-trinitarian understandings of the nature of God.
children.historicalBackground: Grew in the context of early 19th-century American religious freedom, where several independent leaders claimed direct restoration of the ancient church.

children.name: Latter-day Saints (LDS)
children.summary: The largest Restorationist branch, characterizing itself as the restored church of Jesus Christ, guided by modern revelation and prophecy.
coreBeliefs: Modern Prophethood: The President of the Church is a prophet, seer, and revelator.
Godhead: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three separate, physical beings (God has a body).
Eternal Progression: Human souls can grow eternally in the afterlife.
Temple Ordinances: Baptism for the dead and eternal marriage sealing.
children.historicalBackground: Joseph Smith published the Book of Mormon in 1830, claiming translation from golden plates. Following his martyrdom in 1844, Brigham Young led the pioneer migration to Utah.

children.name: Islam
children.summary: A major monotheistic religion based on the revelations received by the Prophet Muhammad, calling humanity to submit to the will of Allah (the One God).
coreBeliefs: Tawhid: The absolute unity and uniqueness of God (Allah).
Prophethood: Muhammad is the seal (final) of a long line of prophets.
Day of Judgment: Reward or punishment based on actions on Earth.
Five Pillars: Testimony of Faith (Shahada), Prayer (Salah), Alms (Zakat), Fasting (Sawm), Pilgrimage (Hajj).
children.historicalBackground: Revelations began in Mecca via the Angel Gabriel to Muhammad. After the Hijra (migration) to Medina in 622 CE, Islam expanded rapidly throughout the Middle East, North Africa, and Persia, split into Sunni and Shia branches over succession.

children.name: Sunni Islam
children.summary: The largest branch of Islam, representing 85-90% of Muslims, which accepts the first four caliphs as the rightful successors to Muhammad.
coreBeliefs: Authority of the Sunnah (Prophetic customs) as compiled by early scholars.
Leadership should be decided by consensus and community choice.
Six Articles of Belief: Belief in God, Angels, Books, Prophets, Day of Judgment, Divine Decree.
children.historicalBackground: Following Muhammad's death, the majority of the community supported Abu Bakr as the first Caliph. Sunni theological schools (Ash'ari, Maturidi) and legal schools developed during the Abbasid Caliphate.

children.name: Shia Islam
children.summary: The second-largest branch of Islam, holding that Muhammad's family (Ahl al-Bayt) and his son-in-law Ali ibn Abi Talib are his divine and political successors.
coreBeliefs: Imamah: Divine leadership vested in infallible successors from the Prophet's family.
Justice of God (Adalah): Rational basis for moral goodness and divine justice.
Ismah: Infallibility of the Prophets and the Imams.
children.historicalBackground: Arising from the dispute over succession, Shia alignment solidified after the martyrdom of Muhammad's grandson Husayn ibn Ali at the Battle of Karbala (680 CE).

children.name: Twelver Shia
children.summary: The largest Shia sub-branch, believing in twelve divine Imams, the last of whom is in occultation and will return as the Mahdi.
coreBeliefs: The belief in twelve Imams starting with Ali and ending with Muhammad al-Mahdi.
Ghaybah (Occultation): The 12th Imam is alive but hidden by divine decree.
Ijtihad: Guidance by qualified jurists (Maraji) during the occultation.
children.historicalBackground: Formed as the mainstream Shia lineage. Recognized as the state religion of Persia (Iran) under the Safavid Dynasty in 1501 CE.

children.name: Ibadi Islam
children.summary: An early independent branch of Islam, dominant in Oman, that arose prior to the Sunni-Shia division, advocating moderate theological positions.
scriptures: Hadith collections of Al-Rabia ibn Habib
coreBeliefs: Rejection of the Sunni concept of seeing God in the afterlife.
The Quran is created (theological alignment with Mutazilites).
Rulers should be selected on religious merit, regardless of tribal lineage.
children.historicalBackground: Emerged from the moderate Muhakkima movement. Separated early from both Sunni caliphates and Shia allegiances, establishing an enduring national presence in Oman and parts of North Africa (Zanzibar, Nafusa mountains).

children.name: Sufism
children.summary: The inner, mystical dimension of Islam, focusing on the purification of the heart, spiritual development, and direct personal experience of God.
children.followersEstimate: Over 100 Million associated with Sufi Orders (Tariqas)
coreBeliefs: Ihsan: Perfecting worship to act as if in direct sight of God.
Tazkiyah: Purification of the self/ego (Nafs) to achieve divine love.
Fana: Annihilation of the individual ego in the Divine Presence.
children.historicalBackground: Began as an ascetic reaction against the wordliness of the early Umayyad Caliphate. It formalized into structured brotherhoods (Tariqas) under spiritual guides (Shaykhs) by the 12th century, playing a key role in spreading Islam.

children.name: Bahá'í Faith
children.summary: A modern monotheistic religion teaching the essential worth of all religions and the unity of all people.
coreBeliefs: Unity of God: There is only one creator deity who is unknowable.
Unity of Religion: All major world religions share a single divine source.
Unity of Humanity: All humans are equal and must establish global peace and justice.
children.historicalBackground: Developed from the Bábí movement in Persia. Bahá'u'lláh declared himself in 1863 to be the divine messenger foretold by the Báb. Faced severe persecution in Iran, establishing its administrative seat in Haifa, Israel.

children.name: Indian Religions (Dharmic)
children.summary: Religions that originated in the Indian subcontinent, sharing core concepts such as Dharma (cosmic order), Karma (cause and effect), Samsara (cycle of rebirth), and Moksha/Nirvana (liberation).
coreBeliefs: Karma: Actions have moral consequences that determine future rebirths.
Samsara: The continuous cycle of birth, life, death, and rebirth.
Dharma: Living in alignment with cosmic law, duty, and ethics.
Moksha / Nirvana: Escape from the cycle of rebirth and achieving spiritual liberation.
children.historicalBackground: Arising out of the Vedic traditions and the subsequent Sramana movements of the 6th century BCE, these religions share vocabulary and philosophical roots while diverging on social caste, scripture authority, and the nature of the self.

children.name: Hinduism
children.summary: A complex synthesis of diverse Indian philosophies, rituals, and traditions, often referred to as Sanatana Dharma (the Eternal Law).
coreBeliefs: Brahman: The ultimate, formless reality or supreme absolute.
Atman: The eternal individual soul, which is fundamentally connected to Brahman.
Purusharthas: Four goals of life (Dharma, Artha/prosperity, Kama/pleasure, Moksha/liberation).
Avatara: The descent of the divine (especially Vishnu) to restore cosmic order.
children.historicalBackground: Formed through the synthesis of local folk beliefs, Vedic traditions, and philosophical systems like Vedanta. It survived waves of foreign influence and reformed via the Bhakti (devotional) movement.

children.name: Vaishnavism
children.summary: A major Hindu branch that considers Vishnu or his avatars (such as Krishna and Rama) as the Supreme Lord.
coreBeliefs: Vishnu is the absolute, personal Supreme God.
Bhakti Yoga (loving devotion) is the supreme path to liberation (Moksha).
Vishnu descends in active avatars to defend righteousness.
children.historicalBackground: Synthesized the worship of historical avatars Krishna and Rama with the Vedic deity Vishnu, heavily popularized by South Indian Tamil poet-saints (Alvars).

children.name: Shaivism
children.summary: A major Hindu branch that considers Shiva as the Supreme Being, focusing on ascetic practices, yoga, and monistic philosophy.
coreBeliefs: Shiva is the supreme ruler, both immanent and transcendent.
Pati-Pashu-Pasha: Lord (Pati), Soul (Pashu), and Bondage (Pasha).
Self-realization is union with the consciousness of Shiva.
children.historicalBackground: Developed from the Vedic storm-deity Rudra. Popularized in South India by the Nayanar poet-saints and philosophically structured by monists like Abhinavagupta in Kashmir.

children.name: Buddhism
children.summary: A major world religion and philosophical system focused on spiritual liberation and the elimination of suffering through ethical living, mindfulness, and meditation.
coreBeliefs: Four Noble Truths: Suffering exists; it stems from craving; it can end; the path is the Eightfold Path.
Noble Eightfold Path: Right view, resolve, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration.
Anatta: The doctrine of non-self; there is no permanent, unchanging soul.
Anicca: Impermanence; all conditioned things are in constant flux.
children.historicalBackground: Founded by Prince Siddhartha Gautama after achieving enlightenment under the Bodhi tree. It spread across Asia via royal patronage (Emperor Ashoka), separating into traditionalist (Theravada) and universalist (Mahayana) branches.

children.name: Theravāda Buddhism
children.summary: The 'School of the Elders,' representing the oldest surviving orthodox school of Buddhism, emphasizing personal monastic liberation.
coreBeliefs: Strict adherence to the original teachings of the historical Buddha.
The goal is to become an Arhat (a liberated saint) who escapes Samsara.
Monastic community (Sangha) is central to practicing the Dharma.
children.historicalBackground: Established as the dominant faith in Sri Lanka and subsequently spread to Southeast Asia, where it became the state religion of Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, and Cambodia.

children.name: Mahāyāna Buddhism
children.summary: The 'Great Vehicle,' which expanded Buddhist doctrine to emphasize the path of the Bodhisattva—seeking enlightenment for the salvation of all sentient beings.
coreBeliefs: Bodhisattva Ideal: Postponing entry into Nirvana to help all others achieve it.
Sunyata: Emptiness; all phenomena are empty of self-nature and exist dependently.
Buddha-nature: Every sentient being possesses the potential to become a Buddha.
children.historicalBackground: Emerged as a reform movement advocating for lay participation. It traveled along the Silk Road to China, Korea, Vietnam, and Japan, adapting local practices (Taoism/Shinto) along the way.

children.name: Sikhism
children.summary: A monotheistic Indian religion emphasizing belief in the One Creator, equality of all humanity, and living a life of truthful conduct and service.
coreBeliefs: Ik Onkar: There is only One Creator God, immanent in all creation.
Equality: Rejection of caste, gender, and racial discrimination.
Three Pillars: Chanting God's name, honest labor, sharing wealth.
The Five Ks: Wearable symbols of faith (Kesh, Kanga, Kara, Kachera, Kirpan).
children.historicalBackground: Founded by Guru Nanak in the Punjab during a period of conflict between Islam and Hinduism. Refined by nine successive human Gurus, the line of leadership ended with Guru Gobind Singh, who designated the scripture as the eternal Guru.

children.name: Iranian Religions
children.summary: Ancient religious movements that emerged from the Iranian plateau, characterized by dualism, ethical choices, and fire rituals.
coreBeliefs: Ethical Dualism: The cosmic battle between Good (Asha) and Evil (Druj).
Free Will: Humans must consciously choose to support cosmic order.
Purity: Keep the natural elements (fire, earth, water) free from defilement.
children.historicalBackground: Evolving from Proto-Indo-Iranian Roots, these systems served as state religions for successive Persian empires, leaving deep theological marks on subsequent monotheistic structures.

children.name: Zoroastrianism
children.summary: One of the world's oldest continuously active religions, originating in ancient Persia, focusing on the wise creator deity Ahura Mazda.
coreBeliefs: Ahura Mazda: The supreme wise creator God who represents pure goodness.
Dualism: Cosmic struggle between Good (Asha) and Evil (Druj).
Humata, Hukhta, Hvarshta: Good Thoughts, Good Words, Good Deeds.
Frashokereti: The ultimate destruction of evil and renewal of the universe.
children.historicalBackground: Founded by the prophet Zoroaster. It was the state religion of three major Persian Empires. Following the Islamic conquest of Persia, many Zoroastrians migrated to India (Parsis).
practices: Praying in front of a sacred fire (Atar)

children.name: East Asian Religions
children.summary: Philosophical and spiritual traditions that developed in China and Japan, characterized by ancestor veneration, harmony with nature, and the concept of Yin and Yang.
coreBeliefs: Harmony: Alignment with the Tao (the Way) or cosmic nature.
Ancestor Worship: Honoring ancestors who watch over descendants.
Yin-Yang: Complementary forces of nature in constant balance.
Filial Piety: Extreme respect for parents, elders, and leaders.
children.historicalBackground: Developed during the Spring and Autumn/Warring States periods of China as answers to social chaos. In Japan, indigenous animist beliefs merged with Chinese imports to form Shinto structures.

children.name: Taoism (Daoism)
children.summary: A religion and philosophy focused on living in harmony with the Tao (the flow of the universe), emphasizing simplicity, naturalness, and spontaneity.
coreBeliefs: The Tao: The undefinable source, pattern, and substance of everything.
Wu Wei: Non-action or effortless action; flowing with the current of nature.
Ziran: Naturalness; being spontaneous and true to one's own nature.
Three Treasures: Compassion, Moderation, and Humility.
children.historicalBackground: Began as a mystical philosophy. During the Han Dynasty, it evolved into an organized religion under Zhang Daoling.

children.name: Confucianism
children.summary: An ethical and philosophical system focusing on filial piety, social order, self-cultivation, and the duty of the individual to the state and family.
coreBeliefs: Ren: Humaneness, benevolence, and love for fellow humans.
Li: Ritual propriety, etiquette, and social norms.
Xiao: Filial piety; deep respect and obedience to one's parents and ancestors.
Mandate of Heaven: The divine right to rule is tied to moral conduct.
children.historicalBackground: Developed during a time of constant warfare to restore social harmony. It became the state ideology under the Han Dynasty, forming the basis of imperial examinations.

children.name: Shinto
children.summary: The indigenous animist religion of Japan, centering on the worship of spirits called Kami that reside in natural phenomena, landscapes, and shrines.
coreBeliefs: Kami: Spiritual entities residing in sacred places, rivers, mountains, and trees.
Kannagara: Living in harmony with the natural order and the Kami.
Purity: Physical and spiritual cleanliness; ritual washing to remove impurities (Kegare).
Matsuri: Direct interaction with Kami through festivals and shrine offerings.
children.historicalBackground: Began as animistic folk practices in ancient Japan. When Buddhism arrived in the 6th century, Shinto was organized to preserve native traditions.

children.name: Ancient Near Eastern Religions
children.summary: The polytheistic religions of the ancient fertile crescent, characterized by temple ziggurats, divine kingship, and agricultural calendars.
coreBeliefs: Polytheism: Pantheon of anthropomorphic deities controlling forces of nature.
Divine state order: Rulers are either divine themselves or absolute emissaries of gods.
Underworld transition: Heavy focus on rituals for the soul's survival after death.
children.historicalBackground: Shaped the earliest city-states and writing systems. They dissolved following the rise of Hellenism and the Roman Empire, eventually replaced by monotheism.

children.name: Ancient European Religions
children.summary: The historical polytheistic and animistic mythologies of Europe, centering on pantheons of sky, earth, and war deities.
children.followersEstimate: Extinct as living traditions; modern reconstructionist groups exist
coreBeliefs: Pantheons led by thunder/sky deities (Zeus, Jupiter, Odin, Perun).
Heroic code: Valor, hospitality, and honor shape spiritual legacy.
Animistic nature spirits (Nymphs, Jotnar, Fairies) inhabit the landscape.
children.historicalBackground: Developed from Indo-European migrations. These traditions shaped the classical philosophy, art, and governance of Western history. Suppressed during Christianization between the 4th and 14th centuries.

children.name: Modern Paganism
children.summary: Contemporary religious movements that reconstruct, revive, or draw inspiration from the historical pagan religions of Europe and the Near East.
coreBeliefs: Nature-centered spirituality: Earth is viewed as sacred or divine.
Pantheism or Polytheism: Veneration of multiple deities or spiritual forces.
Magic (Magick): The use of intent, ritual, and natural energies to effect change.
Reincarnation or cyclical view of life and afterlife.
children.historicalBackground: Grew out of 19th-century romanticism and occult revivals. Wicca was publicized in England in 1954. Reconstructionist groups emerged in the late 20th century, seeking to revive specific historical national cults.

children.name: New Religious Movements
children.summary: Modern spiritual groups and movements that have emerged since the 19th century, characterized by novel doctrines, syncretism, or alternative cosmologies.
coreBeliefs: Revelatory synthesis: Combining scientific metaphors with spiritual concepts.
Universal mission: Focus on creating global harmony or preparing for a new age.
Self-improvement: Utilizing specific practices to unlock human potential.
children.historicalBackground: NRMs often develop in response to rapid scientific advancement and secularization, creating new mythological frameworks that address contemporary human needs.

children.name: Esoteric & Occult Traditions
children.summary: Secret or inner spiritual traditions emphasizing hidden knowledge (gnosis), magical systems, and personal spiritual transmutation.
coreBeliefs: Hermetic Axiom: 'As above, so below' - microcosm mirrors macrocosm.
Esoteric initiation: Spiritual truth is unveiled in progressive degrees.
Alchemical transmutation: Refining the base human soul into divine spirit.
children.historicalBackground: Traced to Alexandria (Egypt) and Gnostic schools. Suppressed by dominant ecclesiastical structures, it survived through underground networks in Renaissance Europe, exploding into the public sphere in the 19th-century occult revival.

children.name: Non-Religious Worldviews
children.summary: Non-theistic, naturalistic, or skeptical philosophical positions explaining existence and ethics without referencing divine revelation.
coreBeliefs: Naturalism: The universe operates entirely via natural laws without divine intervention.
Empiricism: Knowledge is derived from sensory experience and scientific verification.
Human Agency: Humans possess the capability and responsibility to lead ethical lives of personal fulfillment.
children.historicalBackground: Skeptical traditions existed in ancient philosophies (Carvaka in India, Greek materialists). They expanded heavily during the 18th-century European Enlightenment and 20th-century secularization.
